paragraphs.text: Lesson 9, starting a business.
Amy has just started a new company, and she's sharing the news with her friend Beth.
First, listen to their conversation and answer the comprehension questions.
Here it is, my office.
This is a dream come true.
Wow, your very own company.
I can't believe it.
Around the world travel agency is now open for business.
This is…
You've wanted to be a travel agent ever since we were little, and now look at you, I'm so
happy for you.
Hey, if I can do it, you can too.
Have you talked a day about your idea?
I know you're sick of working at the factory.
No, I haven't.
I'm dragging my feet because I'm almost positive you won't like the idea of me starting a catering
business.
You know, money is tight.
Ah, but Beth, you're a great cook.
I mean, I would spend thousands just for a single plate of your spaghetti.
If only I had a hundred eager customers like you.
But starting a business is risky and it could go under at any time.
There are no guarantees.
Dave would never go for it.
Okay, so forget asking Dave.
Well, I can't swing it on my factory salary.
We're barely staying afloat as it is, and I'd need money for supplies, a kitchen, a delivery
truck.
Why not ask your dad?
He's pretty well off.
Oh no, that's out of the question.
He pulled a lot of strings to get me the job I have now in the factory accounting department.
If I tell him I want to quit just to cook food all day, he'll bite my head off.
Alright, I see your point there.
There has to be a way though.
I feel bad having my dream come true knowing that you're slaving away at a job you hate.
I'm okay, really.
I don't mind crunching numbers all day.
But you would rather be crunching walnuts into a delicious dish.
I know you.
Sure, but it's just a pipe dream.
I'd need to win the lottery to make it happen.
Listen, my lunch break is almost over, so…
Not so fast, just let me think.
Better hurry, I have five minutes.
I got it.
We'll go down to the bank and apply for a business loan.
I'll need someone to cosign it though.
I'll get my mother to cosign for you.
She loves you like a daughter, and she would be thrilled to help.
Plus, she'd probably hire you to cater her garden club luncheons.
Oh no, I couldn't ask your mom to cosign on a loan for me.
You don't have to.
I'll talk to her on your behalf.
Listen, we're not getting any younger.
Do you really want to spend the rest of your life pushing papers?
Well, when you put it that way.
Alright, I'm game.
But now I really gotta go back to work.
Give me a call later tonight when I get home from the factory.
Just think.
You'll be putting in your two-week notice before you know it.
Let's take a look at the vocabulary in this conversation.
Amy says, this is a dream come true.
The expression a dream come true refers to something you really wanted to happen, and
then it happened.
Amy asks Beth if she's talked to her husband about her idea for a business.
Amy says, I know you're sick of working at the factory.
To be sick of something does not mean that you are literally physically sick, like you
need a doctor.
I'm sick of it means I'm tired of it.
I'm annoyed with it or I want it to stop.
But Beth says I'm dragging my feet.
The expression dragging my feet means being reluctant or delaying.
The reason Beth is dragging her feet, she says, is because I'm almost positive he won't like
the idea of me starting a catering business.
This phrase I'm almost positive means I'm almost certain.
Beth wants to start a catering business.
The word catering refers to the professional preparation of food for parties and events.
One reason Beth says her husband won't like the idea is money is tight.
Money is tight means we have little money or we have no extra money to spend.
Amy tries to encourage Beth saying that she would spend thousands for just a single plate
of Beth's spaghetti.
Beth replies, if only I had a hundred eager customers like you.
If only means I wish this was the case but it isn't.
And the word eager means excited or enthusiastic.
But, Beth says, starting a business is risky and it could go under at any time.
If a business goes under it means the business fails and loses all its money.
Go under is a more informal way to say go bankrupt.
Beth then says Dave would never go for it.
In this context the word go for it means accept it.
Unfortunately Beth can't swing it on her factory salary.
Can't swing it is an informal phrase meaning can't manage to do it.
Beth and her husband are barely staying afloat as it is.
Staying afloat means surviving with the amount of money we have.
Amy suggests that Beth asks her dad.
Amy says he's pretty well off.
Well off means rich or in a financially comfortable situation.
But Beth says oh no that's out of the question.
That's out of the question means that's not an option or that's not a possibility.
I won't even consider it.
Beth's father pulled a lot of strings to get her the job she has now.
If someone pulls strings it means that person uses their influence to get something done.
Perhaps through some non-official channels.
In this case Beth's father might have known somebody at the company
and used his influence with this person to get his daughter the job.
Beth says if I tell him I want to quit just to cook food all day he'll bite my head off.
This means he'll respond or speak to me very angrily.
Amy says she feels bad having her dream come true knowing that Beth is
slaving away at a job she hates.
The phrasal verb slaving away means working hard as if you were a slave.
Beth says I'm okay really I don't mind crunching numbers all day.
Crunching numbers is a slang way to say doing calculations.
Beth works in the accounting department at the factory so she works with the numbers and calculations.
According to Beth the idea of starting her own business is just a pipe dream.
A pipe dream is an idea that can never happen because it's impossible.
Then Amy has an idea applying for a business loan at the bank.
But Beth responds I'll need someone to cosign it.
Cosign means to sign the contract together.
And Amy says she can get her mother to cosign.
And Amy says she'd probably hire you to cater her garden club luncheons.
The word luncheon refers to a formal lunch or an early afternoon party where lunch is served.
Beth is a bit hesitant to ask Amy's mom for this favor but Amy says you don't have to
I'll talk to her on your behalf.
On your behalf means in your place or for your benefit with your interest in mind.
Then Amy says listen we're not getting any younger.
That's an expression to say we're getting older time is passing so you shouldn't waste time.
Amy asks do you really want to spend the rest of your life pushing papers?
Pushing papers means doing administrative work.
It has the connotation of being boring and rather useless.
Beth is convinced she says well when you put it that way all right when you put it that way means
when you say it like that.
Beth says I'm game that's an informal way to say I'm willing or I'm ready.
At the end of the conversation Beth goes back to work but Amy says just think you'll be putting
in your two week notice before you know it.
The expression putting in your two week notice means informing your employer that you will
quit your job.
This comes from the fact that in the United States it's typical to tell the company two weeks
before you plan to leave permanently.
And the expression before you know it means very soon in the future.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice
and the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
